summary: Lets mail providers publish a policy saying they support TLS-secured SMTP and whether sending servers should refuse to deliver to MX hosts that lack TLS with a trusted certificate. It helps prevent downgrade and interception attacks on email delivery.

eli5.summary: A mailbox owner posts a sign saying only deliver through the locked tunnel, so delivery trucks do not take an unsafe road.

questions: how to force tls for smtp delivery
what is the mta-sts policy file
subtitle: How a mail domain can tell senders: deliver to us only over properly authenticated TLS.

tldr.problem: Opportunistic STARTTLS protects against passive eavesdropping, but an attacker who strips the STARTTLS offer or redirects the SMTP session (for example by overwriting the MX record) can force a downgrade or intercept mail.
tldr.mechanism: A domain publishes a short TXT record at _mta-sts and a policy file over HTTPS. Sending servers fetch and cache the policy, then check each MX host's name and TLS certificate against it before delivering.
tldr.outcome: In enforce mode a sender must not deliver to a host that fails validation, and should retry later instead. The protection depends on the sender having cached a policy and on the Web PKI staying trustworthy.

facts.label: Minimum retry after failed fetch
facts.value: five minutes or longer per version ID

today: RFC 8461 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2018. Its metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, so it remains the definition of MTA-STS. It is meant to be used with TLS reporting (RFC 8460).

sections.title: The Downgrade Problem
sections.content:
The STARTTLS extension to SMTP (RFC 3207) lets mail servers negotiate a TLS channel. On its own it resists passive man-in-the-middle interception, but an attacker who can delete parts of the SMTP session (such as the 250 STARTTLS response) or redirect the whole session (perhaps by overwriting the resolved MX record) can perform downgrade or interception attacks.

MTA-STS lets a recipient domain publish a policy, using a combination of DNS and HTTPS, that says whether sending MTAs can expect PKIX-authenticated TLS support and what they should do with messages when TLS cannot be negotiated. The key terms are the Policy Domain (the next-hop domain, usually the part after the @), the Policy Host (the HTTPS host that serves the policy) and the Sending MTA.
sections.eli5: Locking the mailbox only helps if the mail carrier cannot be tricked into using an unlocked one. MTA-STS lets the family say which locked mailboxes are really theirs.

sections.title: Relation to DANE
sections.content:
DANE TLSA records (RFC 7672) have a similar goal: upgrading unauthenticated encryption or plaintext to authenticated, downgrade-resistant encrypted transmission. DANE needs DNSSEC. MTA-STS relies on certification authorities instead and does not need DNSSEC, at the cost of risking malicious downgrades. Its main motivation is to give domains transport security when deploying DNSSEC is undesirable or impractical.

MTA-STS also has a testing-only mode for soft deployments, which per-MX TLSA records cannot offer in the same way. Where both apply, senders that implement MTA-STS validation MUST NOT let MTA-STS validation override a failing DANE validation.
sections.eli5: There is another way to prove a mailbox is real that uses a special signed phone book. MTA-STS is the option for people who do not have one.

sections.title: Discovering and Fetching a Policy
sections.content:
A sender discovers a policy by resolving one TXT record named _mta-sts at the Policy Domain, for example _mta-sts.example.com. The record holds semicolon-separated fields: v (only STSv1 is supported) and id, a short string that uniquely identifies a policy instance. There is no implied ordering between id values, so a sender can tell whether its cached policy is current just by comparing ids, without any HTTPS request. If there is not exactly one valid record, the sender assumes the domain has no available policy. The record may be a CNAME, which senders MUST follow.

The policy itself is fetched with an HTTPS GET from https://mta-sts.example.com/.well-known/mta-sts.txt. The server's certificate must be valid for the mta-sts name, chain to a trusted root and not be expired. The response is valid only with HTTP 200; redirects MUST NOT be followed and HTTP caching MUST NOT be used. Senders SHOULD check that the media type is text/plain.

If a TXT record exists but no policy can be fetched and there is no valid cached policy, the sender delivers as if MTA-STS were not implemented. If no live policy can be found but a non-expired cached one exists, the sender MUST apply the cached policy. Senders SHOULD proactively refresh cached policies before they expire, with once per day suggested, and alert administrators when refresh fails.

For a smart host, the smart host's domain is the Policy Domain. For mail to a subdomain, senders MUST NOT fetch a policy from the parent zone.
sections.eli5: A small note in the phone book says 'our rules are version 20160831.' If the number matches the rules you wrote down, you do not need to go look them up again.

sections.title: The Policy File
sections.content:
The policy is a set of CRLF-separated key/value pairs, similar to header fields:

  • version: currently only STSv1.
  • mode: enforce, testing or none.
  • max_age: the policy's maximum lifetime in seconds, up to 31557600. Well-behaved clients SHOULD cache a policy for up to this long, and the value is expected to typically be weeks or more.
  • mx: one or more allowed MX host patterns, each on its own line. A pattern is either a full name or a wildcard suffix such as *.example.net.

For internationalized names the mx value MUST be the Punycode A-label. Parsers ignore unknown fields, and if a non-repeated field appears twice, all entries but the first are ignored. Senders MAY limit the fetch with a timeout (one minute is suggested) and a maximum size (64 kilobytes is suggested), and SHOULD wait at least five minutes between failed fetch attempts per version id.
sections.eli5: The rules sheet lists which mailboxes are allowed, how strict to be, and how long to keep the sheet before checking for a new one.

sections.title: Validating and Applying a Policy
sections.content:
When a sender has a valid, non-expired policy, it checks two things for each MX it wants to use. First, at least one mx pattern must match the MX host; a wildcard matches only the whole left-most label, so *.example.com matches mail.example.com but not example.com or foo.bar.example.com. Second, the server must support STARTTLS and present a non-expired certificate that chains to a trusted root and has a DNS-ID subject alternative name matching the host name.

What happens on failure depends on mode:

  • enforce: the sender MUST NOT deliver to hosts that fail MX matching, fail certificate validation or lack STARTTLS.
  • testing: delivery may proceed as if there were no failure, but senders that implement TLSRPT (RFC 8460) send a report of the failure.
  • none: the sender treats the domain as having no active policy.

A message that fails because of an enforce policy MUST NOT be permanently failed before the sender has checked DNS for an updated policy, and such failures should be treated as transient so delivery is retried later. The sender walks the MX candidates in priority order and treats invalid ones as unreachable, rather than prefiltering the list, which can cause message loops.

Senders MUST support the TLS SNI extension, and MTAs must support TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3 or higher.
sections.eli5: Before handing over a letter, the carrier checks that the address is on the approved list and that the door guard shows real ID. In strict mode, no ID means the letter waits and the carrier tries again later.

sections.title: Running MTA-STS
sections.content:
Updating a policy means changing two places: the HTTPS policy body and the TXT record. Recipients SHOULD update the HTTPS body first, so a sender that sees the new TXT record does not cache the old policy. Senders may keep using the old policy until the TXT record's TTL has passed, so old policies should keep working for delivery in the meantime.

To delegate to a mail provider, the Policy Domain points its _mta-sts record at the provider's by CNAME and sends the mta-sts host to the provider, either directly or through a reverse proxy. The endpoint must still present a certificate valid for the Policy Host name itself.

To opt out cleanly, publish a policy with mode none and a small max_age (one day, for example), publish a new TXT record, and remove the TXT record and HTTPS endpoint only after all earlier policies have expired. One caveat of normal MX traversal is that a misconfigured lower-priority backup MX may be discovered only when the primary fails.
sections.eli5: When changing the rules sheet, update the sheet first and then the note saying it changed. To stop using it, post a 'no rules now' sheet and wait for old copies to go stale.

sections.title: What MTA-STS Does Not Stop
sections.content:
MTA-STS aims to stop two attacks: foiling TLS negotiation and impersonating the destination mail server (for example by spoofing the MX record or altering BGP routing tables). It works only if the sender has previously obtained and cached a policy, and only if the attacker cannot obtain a valid certificate that complies with the policy.

The RFC lists specific weaknesses. An attacker who can block DNS responses can hide the policy on first contact or at refresh, so long max_age values and regular background refresh are advised, and DANE does better here thanks to DNSSEC. An attacker who can change a domain's DNS could publish a long-lived malicious policy and cause senders to refuse delivery after the victim fixes its records, though the victim can publish a new policy. A broad pattern such as *.example.com accepts any host with a valid certificate under that domain. Finally, the Web PKI itself, including fraudulently issued certificates and compromised CAs, is a risk that revocation (OCSP, CRLs) only partly addresses.
sections.eli5: The sign only helps if you have seen it before and if nobody can forge the guard's ID. A clever trickster can still hide the sign the very first time.

viz.caption: EXAMPLE TXT RECORD AND POLICY FROM THE RFC

data.title: TXT record and policy
data.code:
_mta-sts.example.com.  IN TXT "v=STSv1; id=20160831085700Z;"

version: STSv1
mode: enforce
mx: mail.example.com
mx: *.example.net
mx: backupmx.example.com
max_age: 604800

messages.label: TXT _mta-sts.example.com
messages.note: One lookup shows whether a policy exists and its id.

messages.label: GET /.well-known/mta-sts.txt
messages.note: Only needed if the id is new.

items.label: Enforce
items.desc: Do not deliver to hosts that fail validation.

items.label: Testing
items.desc: May deliver anyway; send a TLSRPT report if implemented.

items.label: None
items.desc: Treat the domain as having no active policy.
